title: Uninformed search
summary: Breadth-first, depth-first, uniform-cost, and iterative deepening, with the cost hypothesis that makes each one complete or optimal.
intuition:
Uninformed search is the case with no estimate of the remaining cost. The algorithm knows the successors of a node and the cost of a step, and it has no heuristic. Breadth-first search, depth-first search, uniform-cost search, and iterative deepening differ in expansion order and in the memory they keep. Write $b$ for the branching factor, $d$ for the depth of the shallowest goal, and $m$ for the deepest branch the search may follow. Those three letters are not interchangeable.

Breadth-first search expands by depth. When every step costs 1, the first goal it selects for expansion is a shallowest goal, so the path is optimal. The frontier stores a whole level, and both time and space are $O(b^d)$. Depth-first search follows one branch to the end. The stack holds the current path and the untried siblings along it, which is $O(bm)$ space. The goal it returns need not be shallow, and a branch that never ends keeps it from trying the others, so it is not complete on infinite branches.

$$
c(n,a,n')\ge\varepsilon>0
$$

Uniform-cost search expands in order of path cost $g$. Under the hypothesis that every step costs at least some $\varepsilon>0$, it is complete and optimal. The goal test belongs on expansion: the first time the goal is generated can be a costly path, with a cheaper path still sitting in the frontier. Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited depth-first search with limits $0,1,2,\ldots$. Shallow nodes are generated again at every larger limit, and the deepest iteration dominates, so the time is $O(b^d)$ for a unit-cost goal at depth $d$. The space is the depth-first stack, $O(bd)$.

definitions.body: The maximum number of successors of a node, written $b$. A depth-$d$ layer then has on the order of $b^d$ nodes.
A search is complete when a goal at finite depth is eventually expanded, under the cost hypothesis stated for that algorithm.
A search is optimal when the path it returns has the smallest path cost among all paths from the start to a goal. For unit step costs that is a shallowest goal.
The sum of the step costs from the start to the node along the path being considered. Uniform-cost search orders the frontier by $g$.

formulas.name: Breadth-first cost
formulas.note: Unit step costs. Optimal because the first goal expanded has minimum depth.

formulas.name: Depth-first space
formulas.note: $m$ is the deepest branch followed. Time is $O(b^m)$. Not optimal, and not complete on an infinite branch.

formulas.name: Iterative deepening
formulas.note: Complete and optimal for unit step costs. Shallow levels are repeated; the last iteration dominates the time.

formulas.name: Uniform-cost hypothesis
formulas.note: With that lower bound, uniform-cost search is complete and optimal. Test the goal when it is selected for expansion.

properties: Breadth-first search is complete. It is optimal when every step costs 1. Time and space are both $O(b^d)$.
Depth-first search uses $O(bm)$ space. It is not optimal. It is not complete when some branch is infinite.
Uniform-cost search is complete and optimal when every step costs at least $\varepsilon>0$. Expand in order of $g$, and test the goal on expansion.
Iterative deepening is complete and optimal for unit step costs. Space is $O(bd)$. Time is $O(b^d)$ because the iteration at depth $d$ dominates.

On a graph, record a state when it is first generated so a cycle does not make the search run forever. The unit-cost claims above are about the number of edges on a tree, or about the first time a state is reached.

examples.title: One tree, two goals
examples.prompt: The tree is ordered left to right. $S$ has children $A$ then $B$. $A$ has child $C$, $C$ has child $G_1$, and $B$ has child $G_2$. Both $G_1$ and $G_2$ are goals. Every edge costs 1. Trace breadth-first search and depth-first search. A node is expanded when it is taken off the frontier, and the search stops when the expanded node is a goal.
steps: Breadth-first search expands $S$, then $A$, then $B$. Expanding $A$ puts $C$ on the queue after $B$. Expanding $B$ puts $G_2$ on the queue after $C$. The next expansion is $C$, which puts $G_1$ behind $G_2$.
The next node off the queue is $G_2$. The path is $S-B-G_2$, two edges, cost $2$. $G_1$ is still on the queue at depth $3$ and is not expanded.
Depth-first search, popping the left child first, expands $S$, then $A$, then $C$, then $G_1$. It stops at $G_1$. The path $S-A-C-G_1$ has three edges, cost $3$.
The same tree has an optimal cost of $2$. Depth-first search returned $3$, so this run is not optimal. Breadth-first search returned the unit-cost optimum.
examples.answer: Breadth-first search returns $G_2$ at cost $2$. Depth-first search returns $G_1$ at cost $3$.

examples.title: Uniform cost, and the repeated work in iterative deepening
examples.prompt: A second graph has edges $S\xrightarrow{1}A\xrightarrow{3}G$ and $S\xrightarrow{2}B\xrightarrow{1}G$. Separately, run iterative deepening on the unit-cost tree of the first example, with depth limits $0$, $1$, and $2$.
steps: Uniform-cost search expands $S$ at $g=0$ and generates $A$ at cost $1$ and $B$ at cost $2$. It expands $A$ next. That generates $G$ at cost $1+3=4$.
$B$ is still open at cost $2$, which is less than $4$, so $B$ is expanded next and generates $G$ at cost $2+1=3$. The goal is then expanded at cost $3$. The path $S-B-G$ is optimal.
If the program had returned $G$ at the moment it was first generated, it would have returned cost $4$ and missed $S-B-G$. The goal test is on expansion.

On the unit-cost tree, the depth-$0$ iteration expands $S$ only ($1$ node). The depth-$1$ iteration expands $S,A,B$ ($3$ nodes). The depth-$2$ iteration expands $S,A,C,B,G_2$ ($5$ nodes) and stops at $G_2$. The total is $1+3+5=9$.
examples.answer: Uniform-cost search returns cost $3$. The first generated copy of $G$ had cost $4$. Iterative deepening expands $9$ nodes before it expands $G_2$, and the path cost is $2$.

traps: Calling breadth-first search optimal when step costs are not all $1$. Unequal positive costs are the uniform-cost case.
Calling depth-first search complete on a tree that has an infinite branch to the left of the only goal.
Returning a goal from uniform-cost search at the moment it is generated. On the lesson graph that returns $4$ and the optimum is $3$.
Giving iterative deepening the space bound $O(b^d)$. The space is $O(bd)$. The time is the quantity that stays $O(b^d)$.
Swapping $d$ and $m$. The shallowest goal sits at depth $d$. The deepest branch the search may follow has length $m$, and $m$ can be much larger than $d$.

questions.stem: In a tree, $S$ has children $A$ then $B$, $A$ has child $C$, $C$ has child goal $G_1$, and $B$ has child goal $G_2$. Every edge costs $1$. Breadth-first search expands left to right and stops when the expanded node is a goal. It returns
questions.solution: The answer is **A**, $G_2$ at cost $2$. The expansion order is $S,A,B,C,G_2$. The path $S-B-G_2$ has two unit edges. $G_1$ is generated only when $C$ is expanded, and by then $G_2$ is already at the front of the queue.

questions.stem: Which statement matches the cost hypothesis for uninformed search?
options: Depth-first search is complete on every infinite tree.
Breadth-first search is optimal for arbitrary positive step costs.
Uniform-cost search is complete and optimal when every step costs at least $\varepsilon>0$.
questions.solution: The answer is **C**. Uniform-cost search needs every step cost bounded below by some $\varepsilon>0$; under that hypothesis it is complete and optimal. Depth-first search is not complete on an infinite branch. Breadth-first optimality needs unit costs. Iterative deepening uses $O(bd)$ space.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: Breadth-first search uses $O(b^d)$ time and $O(b^d)$ space.
Depth-first search is optimal when every step costs $1$.
Iterative deepening is complete and optimal for unit step costs, with space $O(bd)$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. Breadth-first search keeps a whole level, hence $O(b^d)$ time and space, and it is the unit-cost optimal algorithm. Depth-first space is $O(bm)$, but the goal it finds need not be shallow, so C is false. Iterative deepening keeps the depth-first stack, $O(bd)$, and for unit costs it returns a shallowest goal.

questions.stem: Edges are $S\xrightarrow{1}A\xrightarrow{3}G$ and $S\xrightarrow{2}B\xrightarrow{1}G$. Uniform-cost search tests a goal when the goal is selected for expansion. Which of the following are true?
options: The cost returned by uniform-cost search is $3$.
The first time $G$ is generated, its path cost is already $3$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Adding the edges gives $1+3=4$ and $2+1=3$. Uniform-cost search expands $A$ before $B$, so $G$ is generated first at cost $4$. It does not stop there: $B$ at cost $2$ is expanded next and produces $G$ at cost $3$, and that copy is the one selected for expansion. D describes the generation event, not the expansion.

questions.stem: A complete $3$-ary tree of depth $2$ counts the root as depth $0$, and every internal node has exactly $3$ children. How many nodes does the tree contain?
questions.solution: The answer is **13**. The levels have $1$, $3$, and $3^2=9$ nodes. The total is $1+3+9=13$, which is also $(3^3-1)/(3-1)=26/2=13$. Breadth-first search generates every one of these nodes if the only goal is the last node at depth $2$.
